scenes.narration: Strip Keiji Nishitani of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. Keiji Nishitani (西谷 啓治, Nishitani Keiji; February 27, 1900 – November 24, 1990) was a Japanese philosopher. In 1924, Nishitani received his doctorate from Kyoto Imperial University for his dissertation "Das Ideale und das Reale bei Schelling und Bergson".

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Keiji Nishitani shows exactly where that breaks. Nishitani was born 1900 in a small town in the Ishikawa prefecture. He was fourteen years old when his father died of tuberculosis, a disease he suffered from too as a child.

What looks like free choice in Keiji Nishitani is older than choice itself. Nishitani received most of his schooling in Tôkyô where he lived with his mother after his father's death. He did not pass the physical examination of the prestigious Daiichi High School and waited another year to attempt to enroll after recovering that year in Hokkaidô.

Nobody designed the part of Keiji Nishitani you experience — it was inherited. In a memoir he writes that he was afflicted by great suffering after the loss of his father. Facing this despair, he decided to take up the study of philosophy.

Every serious account of Keiji Nishitani eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. He writes:My life as a young man can be described in a single phrase: it was a period absolutely without hope... My life at the time lay entirely in the grips of nihility and despair...

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Keiji Nishitani — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. My decision then, to study philosophy was in fact – melodramatic as it might sound – a matter of life and death.In his highschool period he became interested in Zen and especially D. Inspired by Nishida's works, he enrolled into the philosophy department of the Kyoto Imperial University, where he studied under Nishida Kitarō and Tanabe Hajime, both philosophers categorised into the Kyoto School.

The selfish-gene reading of Keiji Nishitani makes it less romantic and far more precise. In comparison to their work, that tended to be more abstract, Nishitani included his own experiences with Zen Buddhism in his work. Another point of distinction is that he did not just use the language of Western philosophy to better articulate his thoughts; he criticised Western ideas from a Buddhist perspective.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. After his graduation in 1924 he taught philosophy at local highschools for eight years and assumed a lectureship in the Ôtani University until 1935. In that time he was interested in Schelling and composed a number of works about him and translated two works of Schelling into Japanese.

The feeling that Keiji Nishitani means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. At the age of 37 he received a scholarship to study under Bergson, but because of Bergson's poor health he was the appointed to go to the University of Freiburg, where he spent two years studying under Heidegger. Nishitani held the principal Chair of Philosophy and Religion at Kyoto University from 1943 until becoming emeritus in 1964.

Nothing in Keiji Nishitani was built for you — it was built for reproduction. At various times Nishitani was a visiting professor in the United States and Europe. His themes of teaching did not differ in the philosophy and religion department, because in Japanese thought these are not easily distinguishable.

The psychology underneath Keiji Nishitani is simpler and older than the story on top. As years passed he focused more and more on Buddhist themes and rather used Western ideas to elucidate them. In the years after the Second World War Nishitani's interest with the topic of nihilism coincided with a resurgence of concern in Europe with the very same topic.

Behind Keiji Nishitani sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. In 1949 Nishitani discussed the topic of nihilism in a small group and shortly after composed more and more writings about the topic resulting in his book nihirizumu. On Heisig's reading, Nishitani's philosophy had a distinctive religious and subjective bent, drawing Nishitani close to existentialists and mystics, most notably Søren Kierkegaard and Meister Eckhart, rather than to the scholars and theologians who aimed at systematic elaborations of thought.

The nihilist does not deny Keiji Nishitani — he only refuses to flatter it. Heisig further argues that Nishitani, "the stylistic superior of Nishida," brought Zen poetry, religion, literature, and philosophy organically together in his work to help lay the difficult foundations for a breaking free of the Japanese language, in a similar way to Blaise Pascal or Friedrich Nietzsche. Nishitani's thoughts are also shaped by his study of Western philosophy from the perspective of an outsider, being a person who has grown up in Japan.

What culture calls destiny in Keiji Nishitani is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. This enabled him to view Western philosophy in a distanced mode with respect to his own culture. In Nishitani's view most Western philosophy deals superficially with phenomena of consciousness, and thereby fails to comprehend the depth of our interactions with people and things.

The genes do not care about Keiji Nishitani; they care about copies. In Nishitani's thought there are three fields: the Field of Consciousness, the Field of Nihility, and the Field of Emptiness. These fields are always present alongside each other and each deeper field encompasses the one before.

Take away the meaning and Keiji Nishitani still functions — that is the disturbing part. The Field of Consciousness is the field we experience the world in our everyday life in, the Field of Nihility the one in which we confront death and the Field of Emptiness the one in which both life and death are integrated. Nishitani's criticism of Western philosophy is that it has always been conducted on the Field of Consciousness, where there is no access to a thing in itself but only a representation of it.

The unconscious does not argue with Keiji Nishitani; it simply acts first. This is because we take ourselves as a subject looking upon something as an object in our consciousness. On the Field of Emptiness, that Buddhist practice aims towards, things are encountered on their home-ground.

Keiji Nishitani feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. Furthermore, he sees Kant's thought as emblematic for Western thought and its cultures and civilisations. Kant divides reality into immaterial, invisible, subjective consciousness and material, visible objectivity.

The bleak reading of Keiji Nishitani is also the most testable one. This dualism is most apparent within Christianity in the ethics of an absolute good and absolute evil, right versus wrong and other sharp distinctions. In Nishitani's Buddhist inspired thinking the concept of dependent arising plays an important part: everything is dependent on countless other causes and conditions.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Keiji Nishitani. This logic inspires the inherent logic of the Western world that unfolds into the modern scientific view. Especially, in the works of Nietzsche, Heidegger and Sartre this philosophy of nihility becomes apparent.

The self that experiences Keiji Nishitani is a committee, not a king. In Nishitani's view, it becomes impossible for the Western world to create meaning from their dualistic and Christian foundations. This idea is portrayed in Descartes's res cogitans (consciousness), i.e. the self, and res extensa (extended matter), the things around the self, that are differentiated.

Reproduction explains more of Keiji Nishitani than any philosophy dares to admit. The res cogitans is taken as the ultimate reality that cannot be doubted, while the res extensa remains without true connection to the res cogitans. This lays the foundation for the natural sciences that treat the world as a lifeless mechanism, material to be used for the self.

Once you see Keiji Nishitani as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. He sees machinery as the ultimate appropriation of the laws of nature by people and the assertion of a distinguished self. In his first work "A Philosophy of Elemental Subjectivity" published in 1940 Nishitani elucidates his understanding of religion which he sees as an awareness of elemental subjectivity.

The story Keiji Nishitani tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. By calling it "elemental" he contrasts it with the term "fundamental" as something that has no foundation at all. In order to break this contradiction one needs to realise the ground of one's freedom and transcendence to be a form of self-deception, isolating oneself from all other things.

Meaning is not found in Keiji Nishitani — it is manufactured for it. Out of this naturalness a new subjectivity emerges that is outside of categories like good and bad. This subjectivity signals a return to this life in a nothingness beyond being, in a godhead beyond God.

The cold light on Keiji Nishitani leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. In this field things are experienced within a consciousness that poses oneself as the subjects and other things as objects. Nishitani states that in this field we are unable to encounter things in themselves, in their own mode of being.

Keiji Nishitani did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. Moreover, we cannot just get into touch with objects but also ourselves. This is because this field is separated from things, one's emotions, thoughts and desires.

The honest version of Keiji Nishitani starts by giving up the comforting part. People usually stay within this field distracting themselves from the nihility in life distracting themselves in everyday things. The nihility is confronted again when boredom and the meaninglessness of existence rise up again.

Strip Keiji Nishitani of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. In the field of nihility the existence of all things, including the self, are turned into a great question mark. This concept is similar to the "Great Death" in Zen Buddhism, that heralds the death of the illusion of the self.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Keiji Nishitani shows exactly where that breaks. Within this transformation the world becomes entrenched with the death, because one realises that everything is impermanent. Nishitani connects this to Heidegger's concept of "being-towards-death"–the encounter with death that most profoundly highlights the question of Being.

What looks like free choice in Keiji Nishitani is older than choice itself. The field of nihility is necessary to transition to the field of emptiness, because nihility is needed in order to convert to a perception of reality grounded on śūnyatā, the Buddhist concept of emptiness. The emptiness of nihility is then emptied itself, resulting in an 'absolute emptiness.' This conversion does not take place willingly, as there is no self anymore to exercise a type of will.

Nobody designed the part of Keiji Nishitani you experience — it was inherited. One sees all phenomena as a web of circuminsessional interpretation that links all things together. The field of emptiness is best achieved by eliminating our ignorance and practising meditation.

Every serious account of Keiji Nishitani eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. This is inspired by Dōgen's Zazen practice and his idea of "body-and-mind dropping off." Moreover, a type of thinking of the existential kind can support the transition into the Field of Emptiness. With this type of practice the self has a free access to reality that enables true joy with every interaction.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Keiji Nishitani — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. Nishitani criticises Christianity for the chasm existing between God and his creation, that comes from the dualistic world view of Christianity. He defines God as a godhead which is unknowable, and interpenetrates the deepest human essence while it is interpenetrated by the human essence as well.
